Status epilepticus Although status epilepticus has been defined as continuous or repeated seizure activity lasting 30 minutes or more without any regaining of normal consciousness, current definitions generally consider it to be any continuous sei- zure of more than 5 minutes, or 2 or more seizures without regaining normal consciousness.1-8 Although status may occur with any seizure type, generalised convulsive status is the most common clinical presentation,4 with an esti- mated mortality rate of about 20%; it is most frequent in young children and the elderly.2,3,9 It is a medical emergen- cy, and the longer seizures continue, the more difficult they are to control and the higher the morbidity and mortality; permanent neuronal damage can occur after 30 minutes of seizure activity.7 Management of status epilepticus varies slightly between centres and countries, but the general principles seem to be fairly well established.1-11 • In initial management, it is important to secure the air- way and give oxygen as required, assess cardiac and res- piratory function, and establish intravenous access. Blood glucose should be assessed and any hypoglycae- mia corrected with glucose; intravenous thiamine should be given if there is any suggestion of alcohol abuse or inadequate nutrition.3-6,8,11 • Initial antiepileptic treatment is usually with a benzodi- azepine. Although diazepam has been widely used in the past, intravenous lorazepam is now preferred for first-line treatment in most protocols,1-6,8-12 as it appears to be more effective and has a longer duration of antiep- ileptic action.6,8,12 Rectal diazepam or buccal mida- zolam may be used in the home setting or where intra- venous access is not available.4,5,13 (Rectal diazepam may also have a role in this setting to treat acute repeti- tive seizures,14 which may evolve into status epilepti- cus.)
